intro.objective: Identify terminating and recurring decimals. Write recurring decimals using dot notation. Convert fractions to recurring decimals and convert recurring decimals back to fractions.
commonMistakes: Writing 0.333… as 0.3 — it's recurring, so use dot notation: 0.3̇
Putting dots on the wrong digits — 0.166666… = 0.16̇ (dot only above the 6).
When converting back: forgetting to subtract the equations properly.
methodSteps: Step 1: Divide numerator by denominator using long/short division.
Step 2: If the remainder repeats, the decimal recurs — note which digits repeat.
Step 3: Write using dot notation — one dot over a single repeating digit, two dots over the first and last of a repeating block.
Step 4: To convert recurring decimal → fraction: let x = the decimal, multiply to shift digits, subtract.

methodReminder: 1  Divide top by bottom — look for repeating remainders
2  If it repeats, use dot notation
3  One dot = single digit repeats; two dots = block repeats
4  To convert back: let x = decimal, multiply, subtract

questions.content:
State whether each fraction gives a terminating or recurring decimal.

   a) 1/4       b) 1/3       c) 3/8       d) 2/9

Convert to decimals. Write using dot notation if they recur.

   a) 1/6       b) 1/9       c) 5/6       d) 1/11

Write these using dot notation:

   a) 0.666…       b) 0.142857142857…       c) 0.8333…       d) 0.454545…

Convert to fractions (no working required for these common ones):

   a) 0.1̇       b) 0.3̇       c) 0.9̇

Convert 0.4̇5̇ (0.454545…) to a fraction.
Show all working using the 'let x = …' method.

Convert 0.12̇ (0.1222…) to a fraction.
Hint: this is trickier — the 1 doesn't recur, only the 2 does.

a) Show that 0.0̇9̇ = 1/11.
   b) Hence write 0.6̇3̇ as a fraction.
   c) Is there a pattern for ninths? Complete: 1/9 = ___, 2/9 = ___, 3/9 = ___, …, 8/9 = ___

Prove algebraically that 0.9̇ = 1.

A student says 'it is close to 1 but never reaches it.' Explain why the algebraic proof shows they are equal.

answers.title: Teacher key
rows: Q1: a) Terminating (0.25)  b) Recurring (0.333…)  c) Terminating (0.375)  d) Recurring (0.222…)
Q4: a) 1/9  b) 1/3  c) 1 (accept 9/9 with explanation)
Q8: x = 0.999…; 10x = 9.999…; 10x − x = 9; 9x = 9; x = 1. The proof uses valid algebra — there is no gap between 0.999… and 1; they represent the same number.
